description: ACT / WAIT / HEDGE decision frames for the DECISION screen (SPEC §2 Screen B, §6; MATH_MODEL §8; issue #45). Each frame turns one type of forecast question into a business decision for the fictional demo business in demo_business.json: what happens to the business if the event happens (YES) or not (NO), and three pre-declared policies with every fee stated. The business is SYNTHETIC (not a real company). The shocks and policies are ILLUSTRATIVE modelling choices, not forecasts, not advice and not trading positions.
status: Signed off by Yaseen (finance owner), 2026-11-14 (issue #88): every frame's levers, fees and amounts, the MATH_MODEL §8 break-even formula, and conventions.payroll (no policy cuts payroll; every frame runs with protect_payroll = true; that open question is answered), after the review in docs/FINANCE_REVIEW.md. The sign-off also covers the stock-out version of these frames in PR #141 (#103: stock-out cost and the Fed frame's 1% demand effect, with sigma = 1, theta = 0.20, c_u = 0.01, restaurant sigma = 0.5). Known open points, not blocking: F5 (the Fed frame assumes the planned cut even where the market priced a hold at the cutoff), F7 (the break-even compares only the top two plans), F8 (the supply frame uses a 3-week outage; the synthetic case resolves on 5+ days). Every number below is traceable to a stated assumption or to the MATH_MODEL §10 parameters.
payoff: V(a, y) = min_t C_t, the lowest simulated cash balance over the 26-week horizon, from core.financials.simulate() (MATH_MODEL §8). E[V | a] = p V(a, 1) + (1 - p) V(a, 0). The recommendation is the policy with the largest E[V] among policies feasible in both states (core.decision.evaluate_policies). Payoffs are SIMULATED cash balances of a SYNTHETIC business, never trading P&L.

conventions.week_1: Week 1 of the 26-week plan is the week the question resolves (the FOMC meeting, the CPI release, the start of the disruption window). The plan is fixed at the knowledge cutoff, before week 1.
conventions.ex_ante: Every policy is one fixed ActionPlan applied unchanged in both states: it is decided before any outcome is known and cannot react to it.
conventions.planning_path: The demo business's 8.0% all-in floating rate and flat demand are the CFO's planning path. Each shock is stated relative to that path, so the NO state of a frame can be the plan itself (an empty shock).
conventions.actions_available: Policies may only use the MATH_MODEL §4 actions in ActionPlan: backup supplier, defer capex, delay expansion, purchase cuts, revolver draw/repay, payroll cut. The model has no interest-rate swaps, caps or other financial hedges, so no policy here is a financial hedge or a trading position.
conventions.capex_and_expansion: The demo business has K_t = 0, E_t = 0 and X_t = 0 (MATH_MODEL §10 'set per demo case'), so 'defer capex' and 'delay expansion' would change nothing. No policy uses them, and frames do not override the business.
conventions.payroll: Proposal: no policy cuts payroll (z_t = 0 everywhere) and every frame is evaluated with protect_payroll = true. Open question for the finance owner.
conventions.purchase_cuts: Total cuts stay well under I_0 - I_min = 65,000 - 40,000 = 25,000, and each weekly cut is far below normal purchases of (1 - g) x 50,000 = 32,500 a week, so purchases and inventory stay positive. A purchase cut is not free cash (issue #103, MATH_MODEL §3): inventory below the service level I^svc_t = I_0 x m_t (65,000 at planned demand, scaled by the demand multiplier m_t) loses 0.20 of sales per $ of shortfall per week, so a cut pays only when lower demand is expected to lower the stock the business needs.
conventions.fees: Each fee lists whether it is in the payoff. Cash costs (switching fee F_b, backup premium, revolver interest J^R_t, extra term-loan interest) are in the simulated cash path. The MATH_MODEL §10 disruption costs c_. are non-cash harm and are NOT in V; they are listed so nothing is hidden. Stock-out lost margin (issue #103) is a cash effect, so it is in the payoff; its typed amount is checked against the engine as V(a, y) with the stock-out cost switched off (theta = 0) minus V(a, y).

schema.frames[].question_template: The question with {placeholders} filled per case.
schema.frames[].yes_means / no_means: What y = 1 and y = 0 mean in plain words.
schema.frames[].no_state_models: Which NO outcome shock_if_no models. If the case resolves NO in a way the frame does not model, the reveal shows not_modelled_note (when present) instead of a regret.
schema.frames[].not_modelled_note: Optional. The NOT AVAILABLE text shown at reveal for an unmodelled NO outcome.
schema.frames[].forecast_sensitive: true if the recommended policy changes as P(YES) goes from 0 to 1 (a break-even p* exists); tested against the engine.
schema.frames[].caveat: Required when forecast_sensitive is false: one line saying the recommendation does not depend on the forecast, and why.
schema.frames[].assumptions: Every assumption behind the shocks, labelled ILLUSTRATIVE.
schema.frames[].shock_rationale: Why each shock is what it is, with the arithmetic.
schema.frames[].policies[]: Exactly ACT, WAIT and HEDGE. name + summary + plan build a core.decision.Policy (description = summary).
schema.frames[].policies[].fees[]: {item, amount, when, in_payoff}: every cash and non-cash cost of the policy.

frames.question_template: Will the FOMC leave the federal funds target range unchanged at its {meeting} meeting?
frames.yes_means: The Fed holds: the target range is left unchanged.
frames.no_means: The Fed changes the range: a cut or a hike (the replay cases' rule is NO if either bound changes). This frame models only the cut: shock_if_no is the 25bp cut the planning path already assumes. If NO turns out to be a hike, this frame has no payoff for it and the reveal shows not_modelled_note instead of a regret.
frames.not_modelled_note: NOT AVAILABLE: this frame does not model a hike
assumptions: ILLUSTRATIVE: the CFO's planning path (the 8.0% all-in floating rate in demo_business.json) already assumes a 25bp cut at this meeting, as if markets expected a cut. If a real case's market priced a hold at the cutoff, the shocks must be re-anchored for that case.
ILLUSTRATIVE: the 600,000 floating term loan reprices from week 2, the week after the decision.
ILLUSTRATIVE: a hold is a one-step +25bp gap to the plan that persists to week 26 (no later catch-up cut is modelled).

ILLUSTRATIVE (proposal for finance-owner review, issue #103): a hold keeps household borrowing costs above what was planned and a small share of customers of a fresh/deli-heavy grocer trade down, so base-store demand is 1% below the plan from week 2 to week 26 (a third of the CPI frame's 3% hot-print effect, and persistent like the rate gap). Without a demand channel no available action's payoff depends on the rate, so ACT, WAIT and HEDGE would differ by the same amount in both states and no break-even p* could exist (MATH_MODEL §8).
The revolver is undrawn in every policy here, so only the term loan carries the rate shock.

shock_if_yes.name: Fed holds: floating rate 25bp above the plan and demand 1% below it from week 2

shock_if_no.name: Fed cuts 25bp as planned: planning path, no shock

shock_rationale.if_yes: Rate: the plan assumed a cut that does not come, so the floating rate is 8.25% instead of 8.0% from week 2: extra interest 600,000 x 0.25% / 52 = 28.85 a week, x 25 weeks (2..26) = 721.15. Demand: 1% of 50,000 = 500 of sales lost a week in weeks 2-26. By week 26 receipts have lost 500 x 25 - 0.2 x 500 (week 26's late-paid 20% arrives in week 27) = 12,400 and payables have fallen by 0.65 x 500 x 23 (purchases of weeks 2-24, paid two weeks later) = 7,475, so 4,925. Total: 721.15 + 4,925 = 5,646.15 lower cash by week 26.
shock_rationale.if_no: The cut the plan assumed happens, so the business follows its planning path: no shock.

policies.name: ACT
policies.summary: Cut purchases by 650 in week 2, bringing stock down to the lower service level a hold would bring.
policies.rationale: The service level is I^svc_t = I_0 x m_t = 65,000 x m_t, i.e. 2 weeks of cost of goods at planned demand (MATH_MODEL §3): 65,000 at planned demand, 64,350 if demand is 1% lower. If the Fed holds, 650 of stock becomes surplus and cutting it releases 650 of cash with no stock-out. If the Fed cuts as planned, the same cut leaves inventory 650 below the 65,000 service level in weeks 2-26 and loses 0.20 x 650 = 130 of sales a week; by week 26 that has cost 130 x (0.35 x 23 + 1.0 + 0.8) = 1,280.50 of cash (a lost sale in weeks 2-24 costs the 35% margin once settled; in week 25 the saved purchase would be paid only after week 26, so it costs the full sale; in week 26 the 80% collected that week). Net +650 if the Fed holds, 650 - 1,280.50 = -630.50 if it cuts. A real CFO with a floating-rate loan might instead buy an interest-rate cap or swap; this model has no such instrument.

fees.when: weeks 2-26, NO only (none if the Fed holds: the stock then matches the lower service level)

fees.item: Purchase-cut disruption cost c_v (MATH_MODEL §10)
Stock-shortfall disruption cost c_u (MATH_MODEL §10, issue #103)

policies.name: WAIT
policies.summary: Change nothing and carry the floating-rate exposure.
policies.rationale: Keep stock at the 65,000 service level. If the Fed holds, the business carries the higher interest and the lower demand (5,646.15 lower cash by week 26, about 9% of the planning path's lowest balance of 63,000) with 650 of stock it no longer needs; if it cuts, nothing is lost. Waiting keeps every lever available for later.

fees.item: Extra term-loan interest if the Fed holds
Lost gross margin on lower demand if the Fed holds

policies.name: HEDGE
policies.summary: Cut purchases by 325 in week 2: half of ACT.
policies.rationale: A half-size commitment. If the Fed holds, 325 of surplus stock is released (+325); if it cuts, inventory sits 325 below the service level and loses 0.20 x 325 = 65 of sales a week, 65 x 9.85 = 640.25 of cash by week 26 (net -315.25). Its payoffs are exactly halfway between ACT and WAIT in both states, so it ties with both at the break-even p* and is never strictly best. This is not a financial hedge: the model has no rate caps or swaps.

frames.yes_means: A hotter print than the threshold: inflation is running above what the plan assumed.
frames.no_means: An in-line or cooler print. This frame treats NO as the planning path (no upside shock from a cooler print is modelled).
frames.no_state_models: in-line or cooler print, both treated as the planning path
assumptions: ILLUSTRATIVE: the planning path assumes an in-line print and a 25bp cut at the next FOMC meeting, about 3 weeks after the release.
ILLUSTRATIVE: a hot print pushes that cut out, so the floating rate stays 25bp above the plan from week 4 to week 26.

ILLUSTRATIVE: a hot print signals a real-income squeeze; some customers of a fresh/deli-heavy grocer trade down to discounters, so base-store demand is 3% lower in weeks 3-14 (one quarter), then recovers linearly over 4 weeks.
Not modelled: inflation in the business's own prices and costs. Gross margin g and baseline sales are fixed in BusinessParams, so the frame captures only the rate and real-demand channels.
The revolver is undrawn in every policy here, so only the term loan carries the rate shock.

shock_if_yes.name: Hot CPI print: rate +25bp vs plan from week 4, demand -3% weeks 3-14

shock_if_no.name: In-line or cooler CPI print: planning path, no shock

shock_rationale.if_yes: Rate: 600,000 x 0.25% / 52 = 28.85 a week, x 23 weeks (4..26) = 663.46. Demand: 3% of 50,000 = 1,500 of sales a week for 12 weeks = 18,000, plus the recovery m_t = 1 - 0.03 (1 - k/4) for k = 1..4 losing 1,125 + 750 + 375 + 0 = 2,250, so 20,250 of lost sales; each lost sales dollar costs the 35% gross margin once receipts and payables settle (by week 20): 0.35 x 20,250 = 7,087.50. Total: about 7,750.96 lower cash by week 26.
shock_rationale.if_no: The print is in line with the plan (or cooler, treated the same), so the business follows its planning path: no shock.

policies.name: ACT
policies.summary: Cut purchases by 975 in week 3: half of the 1,950 drop in the service level a hot print would bring.
policies.rationale: The service level is I^svc_t = I_0 x m_t = 65,000 x m_t, i.e. 2 weeks of cost of goods at planned demand (MATH_MODEL §3): 65,000 at planned demand; after a hot print 63,050 in weeks 3-14 (3% lower), then 63,537.50, 64,025 and 64,512.50 in weeks 15-17 as demand recovers, and 65,000 again from week 18. A cut is permanent (the model has no restocking action), so stock cut below 65,000 is short again once demand recovers. ACT leaves inventory at 64,025. Hot print: short by 487.50 in week 17 and 975 in weeks 18-26, losing 0.20 of sales per $ short; by week 26 that costs 0.35 x (97.50 + 7 x 195) + 195 x 1.0 + 195 x 0.8 = 862.88, so net 975 - 862.88 = +112.13. In-line print: short by 975 in weeks 3-26, 195 of sales a week, 195 x (0.35 x 22 + 1.0 + 0.8) = 1,852.50, so net -877.50. A real CFO might also hedge the floating rate with a cap or swap; this model has no such instrument.

policies.name: WAIT
policies.summary: Change nothing and absorb the hot-print hit if it comes.
policies.rationale: Keep stock at the service level. Even a hot print leaves the lowest cash balance far above the 25,000 floor (about 63,000 - 7,751 = 55,249). If the print is hot, the business holds up to 1,950 of stock it does not need for a quarter; if it is in line, nothing is lost.

policies.name: HEDGE
policies.summary: Cut purchases by 487.50 in week 3: half of ACT.
policies.rationale: The service level is I^svc_t = I_0 x m_t = 65,000 x m_t, i.e. 2 weeks of cost of goods at planned demand (MATH_MODEL §3): 65,000 at planned demand; after a hot print 63,050 in weeks 3-14 (3% lower), then 63,537.50, 64,025 and 64,512.50 in weeks 15-17 as demand recovers, and 65,000 again from week 18. A cut is permanent (the model has no restocking action), so stock cut below 65,000 is short again once demand recovers. HEDGE leaves inventory at 64,512.50. Hot print: short by 487.50 only in weeks 18-26, 97.50 of sales a week, 0.35 x 7 x 97.50 + 97.50 x 1.0 + 97.50 x 0.8 = 414.38, so net 487.50 - 414.38 = +73.13. In-line print: short in weeks 3-26, 97.50 x 9.5 = 926.25, so net -438.75. Per dollar cut it gains more than ACT after a hot print (ACT's second half is short one week longer) and loses the same in line, so it is the best policy for P(YES) between 6/7 = 0.857 and 45/49 = 0.918. This is not a financial hedge: the model has no interest-rate caps, swaps or inflation-linked instruments.

frames.question_template: Will {disruption_event} halt deliveries from the primary distributor during {window}?
frames.yes_means: The disruption happens: the primary distributor cannot deliver for 3 weeks.
frames.no_means: No disruption: the primary distributor delivers as normal.
assumptions: ILLUSTRATIVE: added beyond the two question types named in issue #45 because, before issue #103, the FOMC and CPI frames could not produce a break-even probability (purchase cuts were free cash); a lead may drop it.

ILLUSTRATIVE: the YES state is the supplier-outage-3wk scenario in scenarios.json: the primary distributor is down in weeks 5-7 (availability 0), and 40% of base-store sales depend on it (phi = 0.40, MATH_MODEL §10).
The backup supplier must be signed up at the cutoff (before week 1) to be available in weeks 5-7; it cannot be added after the disruption is known.
No rate or demand effect in either state.

shock_if_no.name: No disruption: planning path, no shock

shock_rationale.if_yes: Without a backup supplier, 40% of 50,000 = 20,000 of base-store sales a week is lost for 3 weeks = 60,000; at the 35% gross margin that is 0.35 x 60,000 = 21,000 lower cash by week 26.
shock_rationale.if_no: The distributor delivers, so the business follows its planning path: no shock.

policies.name: ACT
policies.summary: Sign up the backup supplier now: pay the 2,000 switching fee whatever happens, and the 12% premium only if the disruption hits.
policies.rationale: This is the model's one true insurance-like action: a fixed cost in both states that removes the lost sales if the disruption happens. If YES, the backup supplier keeps the 20,000 a week of outage-share sales but charges 12% more on their cost of goods: 0.12 x 0.65 x 20,000 = 1,560 a week x 3 weeks = 4,680.

fees.item: Backup-supplier switching fee F_b (MATH_MODEL §10)
Backup premium pi on outage-share purchases (MATH_MODEL §10)
fees.when: weeks 5-7 purchases, paid weeks 7-9, YES only

fees.item: Backup-supplier disruption cost c_b (MATH_MODEL §10)

policies.name: WAIT
policies.summary: Change nothing and lose the outage-share sales if the disruption hits.
policies.rationale: No fee is paid. If YES, 60,000 of sales are lost and cash ends 21,000 lower, still above the 25,000 floor (about 42,000).

fees.item: Lost gross margin on outage-share sales

policies.name: HEDGE
policies.summary: Arrange liquidity instead of supply: draw 21,000 on the revolver in week 4 and repay it in week 12.
policies.rationale: Sized to the 21,000 cash hit of the disruption, drawn just before the outage window and repaid after its cash effects settle (week 9). It protects the timing of cash, not the lost margin, and it pays revolver interest in both states: (8.0% + 2.0%) / 52 x 21,000 = 40.38 a week for weeks 5-12 = 323.08. Because the lost margin is permanent and the lowest balance is at week 26 after repayment, this policy can only lower V in this model; it is included to show the carrying cost of a liquidity buffer.
